summary: Children (ages 7–9) learn that a coprolite is fossilised dung — a trace fossil that records an animal's feeding — and that cutting one open can reveal contents (seeds and plant fibres, crushed bone, or fish scales) that give DIRECT evidence of what the animal that produced it actually ate, at least in that meal (mostly the tougher, less-digested parts survive). The central idea is contrasting this with the INDIRECT clue of tooth shape: teeth suggest what an animal COULD eat, while coprolite contents show what it DID eat. Learners practise reading contents to a diet conclusion (seeds→plant-eater, bone→meat-eater, scales→fish-eater), and also meet the honest limit that it is often uncertain WHICH animal produced a given coprolite.
misconceptions: 'A coprolite is a body fossil / a stomach' — it's fossilised dung, a trace fossil recording feeding.
'Coprolites are worthless/just gross' — they are direct, high-value evidence of diet.
'Teeth already tell us exactly what it ate' — teeth show capability; coprolites show actual meals.
'We always know which dinosaur made a coprolite' — attribution is often uncertain.
'All dung fossils look the same inside' — contents differ (plants, bone, scales) and that's the whole point.

activities.title: Slice and examine: read the coprolite's contents
steps: Receive a lumpy grey 'coprolite' specimen and the explanation that it is fossilised dinosaur dung turned to rock.
Open the specimen and sweep a magnifier across the cut face to find embedded contents — seeds and shredded plant fibres in one specimen, splinters of crushed bone in another, fish scales in a third.

Collect each find (optionally by dragging items into an analysis panel) and state the diet verdict it supports: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → bone-crunching meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Write or say the reasoning: 'the contents are the remains of what the animal ate, so this dinosaur was a ___.'
activities.insight: The things preserved inside fossilised dung are the remains of an animal's meals, so reading those contents lets you infer what the dinosaur actually ate.

activities.title: Teeth clue vs dung clue: could eat vs did eat
steps: Look at an animal's teeth beside the contents of a coprolite thought to come from that kind of animal, presented side by side.
Say what the teeth suggest the animal COULD eat (capability) and what the coprolite shows it ACTUALLY ate (its real meals).
Explain in their own words why the coprolite is direct evidence of diet while the teeth are an indirect clue.
activities.insight: Tooth shape suggests what an animal was capable of eating, but coprolite contents are direct evidence of what it really ate — a comparison of indirect versus direct evidence.

activities.title: Whose dung was it? Modelling honest uncertainty
steps: Examine a coprolite with clear contents (e.g. the famous large bone-filled Cretaceous specimen attributed to T. rex) and confidently state the DIET it shows.
Then try to name exactly which animal produced it, and notice how hard that is.
Say out loud what we can be sure of (the diet) and what remains uncertain (the exact producer), and why 'we're not sure' is a valid scientific answer.
activities.insight: Even strong evidence leaves some questions open: coprolite contents can firmly reveal diet while the exact animal that produced the dung often stays uncertain.

activities.title: Check: match contents to diet and explain the evidence
steps: Match coprolite contents to the diet they imply: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Answer: 'What does crushed bone inside a coprolite tell us about the dinosaur that made it?' and explain how you know.
Transfer the reasoning to a new case: a coprolite full of chewed leaves and seeds — what kind of dinosaur made it?
activities.insight: Being able to map contents onto a diet, and explain why, confirms the inference transfers to new specimens.

activities.title: Optional: palaeontologist hands over a specimen
steps: Take a coprolite from an expert who asks, 'What did this animal eat, and how sure are you?'
Describe the contents you can see and reason aloud toward a diet.
Respond to follow-up prompts about how confident you are and whether you can tell which animal made it.
activities.insight: Articulating the inference and your confidence to a questioner strengthens the reasoning and the habit of qualifying claims.

checkQuestion: Scientists cut open a fossilised lump of dinosaur dung and find crushed bones and fish scales inside. What can they tell about the dinosaur that made it, and how do they know?
checkAnswer: It was a meat-eater — it ate animals and fish. The crushed bones and scales inside are the remains of its food, preserved in its fossilised droppings (a coprolite). The contents are direct evidence of what the dinosaur ate.
